## TASK 1,2,3
```{r}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename(title = Title,
           runtime = Runtime,
           views = Views,
           hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
           release_date = `Release Date`,
           available_globally = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year),
           available_globally = available_globally == "Yes")
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

library(skimr)

## TASK 5
```{r}
library(scales)

# Q1: the date range of the data
date_start <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
date_end   <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)

# Q2: how many different titles
n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)

# Q3: hours spent on every Bridgerton title
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q4: Stranger Things hours (leaving out the spin-offs and the Fireplace video)
stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales From")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q5: share of 2026H1 watch time going to the 10 biggest titles
data_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1")

top10_hours <- data_2026 |>
  arrange(desc(hours_viewed)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

top10_share <- top10_hours / sum(data_2026$hours_viewed)

# Q6: how much of the catalog is available everywhere
global_by_title <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally, na.rm = TRUE)

known_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally))

global_hours <- known_data |>
  filter(available_globally) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

global_by_hours <- global_hours / sum(known_data$hours_viewed)
```
1) The data set covers a date range starting from `r month(date_start, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)` `r label_ordinal()(day(date_start))`,`r year(date_start)` and ending at `r month(date_end, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)` `r label_ordinal()(day(date_end))` `r year(date_end)`.

2) The data set covers `r comma(n_titles)` distinct titles.

3) Netflix users have spent `r comma(bridgerton_hours)` hours watching Bridgerton.

4) Netflix users have spent `r comma(stranger_hours)` hours watching the five seasons of stranger things.

5) The top 10 shows on Netflix covered about `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of its total watch time.

6) About `r percent(global_by_title, accuracy = 1)` of Netflix Catalog is globally available and `r percent(global_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)` is globally viewed by the hour.

## TASK 6

### Top Title in Each Period

```{r}
library(gt)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed)) |>   # each title's share of its period
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>  # keep the #1 title in each period
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", title = "Top Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed", share = "Share of Period Viewing") |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```
I divided each title’s hours by its period’s total hours and kept only the #1 title per period, which captured between 0.9% and 1.4% of viewing.

### Catalog Size Over Time

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    n_titles = n_distinct(title),                            # how many titles
    total_runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,   # total length, in hours
    n_missing_runtime = sum(is.na(runtime))                  # titles with no runtime
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", n_titles = "Titles Reported",
             total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (hours)",
             n_missing_runtime = "Titles Missing Runtime") |>
  fmt_number(c(n_titles, total_runtime_hours, n_missing_runtime),
             decimals = 0) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```
I measured catalog size by both distinct titles and total runtime hours, and I base trends on 2023H2 onward because 12,415 of 2023H1’s 18,126 titles have no runtime.

### Consistently Watched Titles

```{r}
# Step 1: summarize each title across all periods
title_summary <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarize(
    n_periods = n_distinct(period),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
    sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed)
  ) |>
  mutate(variability = sd_hours / avg_hours)   # small = steady viewing

all_periods <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

# Step 2: keep steady titles that appear in every period,
#         then take the 10 with the best worst-period
title_summary |>
  filter(n_periods == all_periods) |>
  filter(variability < 0.3) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10) |>
  select(title, avg_hours, min_hours, variability) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(title = "Title", avg_hours = "Avg. Hours per Period",
             min_hours = "Lowest Period (Hours)",
             variability = "Variability (SD / Mean)") |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, min_hours), decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  fmt_number(variability, decimals = 2) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```
I kept titles that appear in all seven periods with variability (SD divided by mean) below 0.3, then ranked them by their lowest-period hours so the list rewards a high floor rather than a one-time spike.

### Shows vs. Movies

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    str_detect(title, "Season") ~ "Show",   # "Season" in the name means a TV show
    runtime > 240 ~ "Show",                 # longer than 4 hours is probably a show
    !is.na(runtime) ~ "Movie",              # everything else with a runtime
    .default = "Unclassified"               # no runtime, so we can't tell
  )) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    Show = sum(hours_viewed[type == "Show"]) / sum(hours_viewed),
    Movie = sum(hours_viewed[type == "Movie"]) / sum(hours_viewed),
    Unclassified = sum(hours_viewed[type == "Unclassified"]) / sum(hours_viewed)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", Show = "Shows", Movie = "Movies",
             Unclassified = "Unclassified (no runtime)") |>
  fmt_percent(c(Show, Movie, Unclassified), decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports; show/movie split is a heuristic")
```
I labeled a title a show if its name contains “Season” or its runtime exceeds 240 minutes, a movie if it has a shorter runtime, and unclassified if it has no runtime, which means the roughly 3% to 4% movie share is approximate.

### Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(live_event) |>
  summarize(
    n_titles = n(),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed),
    # sort biggest to smallest, keep the first 10, then average them
    top10_avg = mean(sort(hours_viewed, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10])
  ) |>
  mutate(live_event = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-Taped")) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(live_event = "Type", n_titles = "Title-Periods",
             avg_hours = "Average Hours", median_hours = "Median Hours",
             top10_avg = "Average of Top 10") |>
  fmt_number(n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, median_hours, top10_avg), decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```
I compared the average, median, and top-10 average for each group, and while typical titles perform about the same (1.7M vs. 1.8M median hours), the best pre-taped titles far outdraw the best live events (791.4M vs. 36.7M) in a live sample of only 310 rows.

## TASK 7

## Supporting Calculations for Strategy Memo

```{r}
# Rank titles within each period (biggest first) and track a running share
ranked_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  arrange(desc(hours_viewed), .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    title_rank = row_number(),
    running_share = cumsum(hours_viewed) / sum(hours_viewed)
  )

# One row per period
period_stats <- ranked_titles |>
  summarize(
    n_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed),
    mean_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed),
    top10_share = sum(hours_viewed[title_rank <= 10]) / sum(hours_viewed),
    titles_for_half = sum(running_share < 0.5) + 1   # titles needed to reach half of all hours
  )

baseline <- period_stats |> filter(period == "2023H2")
latest   <- period_stats |> filter(period == "2026H1")

# Average hours for titles outside each period's top 1%
tail_stats <- ranked_titles |>
  mutate(is_top1pct = title_rank <= ceiling(0.01 * n())) |>
  filter(!is_top1pct) |>
  summarize(mean_outside_top1 = mean(hours_viewed))

tail_base   <- tail_stats |> filter(period == "2023H2")
tail_latest <- tail_stats |> filter(period == "2026H1")
```


## Strategy Memo

**To:** Netflix Leadership\
**From:** Justin Leung\
**Re:** Hold the budget for elsewhere

### Recommendation

Netflix should hold its 2027 title count near 2026H1 levels and redirect their budget towards renewals and larger-budget seasons. From 2023H2 to 2026H1, the catalog grew `r percent(latest$n_titles / baseline$n_titles - 1, accuracy = 1)` but total viewing grew only `r percent(latest$total_hours / baseline$total_hours - 1, accuracy = 0.1)`, so the average title now earns less. Meanwhile, about `r round(latest$titles_for_half, -1)` titles per half-year generate half of all the hours.

### 1. Supply is outrunning demand

Netflix’s supply is growing faster than viewer attention. From 2023H2 to 2026H1, titles reported went from `r comma(baseline$n_titles)` to `r comma(latest$n_titles)` growing about `r percent(latest$n_titles / baseline$n_titles - 1, accuracy = 1)`. While total hours viewed grew only `r percent(latest$total_hours / baseline$total_hours - 1, accuracy = 0.1)` from `r number(baseline$total_hours / 1e9, accuracy = 0.1)` billion to `r number(latest$total_hours / 1e9, accuracy = 0.1)` billion. As a result, mean hours per title fell about `r percent(1 - latest$mean_hours / baseline$mean_hours, accuracy = 1)` from `r number(baseline$mean_hours / 1e6, accuracy = 0.01)` million to `r number(latest$mean_hours / 1e6, accuracy = 0.01)` million. This matters because viewing is growing at roughly `r percent((latest$total_hours / baseline$total_hours - 1) / (latest$n_titles / baseline$n_titles - 1), accuracy = 1)` of the rate of the catalog, so each added title splits a pool of attention that isn’t keeping pace.

### 2. Trends over time

Since Netflix keeps adding new shows, but people aren't watching enough to keep up. Between 2023H2 and 2026H1, the catalog grew `r percent(latest$n_titles / baseline$n_titles - 1, accuracy = 1)`, while total viewing grew only `r percent(latest$total_hours / baseline$total_hours - 1, accuracy = 0.1)`.The average show gets `r percent(1 - latest$mean_hours / baseline$mean_hours, accuracy = 1)` less attention than before. Along with this viewing is especially concentrated in the "top". The top 10 shows account for `r percent(latest$top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of all hours but half of the hours goes to `r latest$titles_for_half` titles. That's only `r percent(latest$titles_for_half / latest$n_titles, accuracy = 0.1)` of all titles. While the average title outside the top 1% fell from `r number(tail_base$mean_outside_top1 / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million to `r number(tail_latest$mean_outside_top1 / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million about a `r percent(1 - tail_latest$mean_outside_top1 / tail_base$mean_outside_top1, accuracy = 1)` decrease.

### Next Steps

1. Stop adding more titles. Keep the total about where it is now (around `r comma(round(latest$n_titles, -3))` per half-year). Adding more has meant each title gets fewer views.
2. Move money away from small, low-performing titles. Put it into bringing back shows that already work and into mid-to-big-budget seasons that can break into the group of ~`r round(latest$titles_for_half, -1)` titles that drives half of all viewing.
3. Judge success with two simple numbers. First, how well the typical title does (the median, now `r number(latest$median_hours / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)`M hours and slipping). Second, how many new titles make it into that ~`r round(latest$titles_for_half, -1)`-title top group.
